name: Pyrexia of Unknown Origin

veryLikely: Diagnosis-dependent — broad differential includes infective (TB, enteric fever, infective endocarditis, abscess), neoplastic (lymphoma), and autoimmune/rheumatologic causes
pathogens.why: PUO is explicitly a syndrome of unknown etiology by definition — pathogen prediction is not applicable until a specific diagnostic lead (localizing symptom, imaging finding, or lab abnormality) narrows the differential. Treating empirically before this risks masking the true diagnosis.

investigations.test: Repeat detailed history and serial examinations
investigations.why: New localizing signs often emerge over time and are the single most valuable step in PUO workup.

investigations.test: CBC, ESR, CRP, LFTs, RFTs, urinalysis
investigations.why: First-tier screening tests that can reveal a localizing clue (e.g., abnormal LFTs pointing to liver abscess or biliary source).

investigations.test: Blood cultures (multiple sets, including for fastidious organisms if endocarditis suspected)
investigations.why: Identifies bacteremic causes including culture-negative endocarditis pathogens with extended incubation.
First-line imaging to screen for occult infection (TB, abscess) or malignancy.
More sensitive for occult abscess, lymphadenopathy, or malignancy if first-tier workup is unrevealing.

investigations.test: Echocardiography (if any murmur, risk factors, or persistent bacteremia)
investigations.why: Screens for infective endocarditis as a cause of prolonged fever.

references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine (Approach to Fever of Unknown Origin)
reason: Fever ≥3 weeks duration without an identified source despite reasonable initial evaluation defines pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO). Empiric antibiotics are NOT indicated in classic PUO without a localizing diagnosis or evidence of toxicity/instability — blind antibiotic trials can obscure the diagnostic picture (e.g., partially treating tuberculosis or culture-negative endocarditis) and delay reaching a true diagnosis. A systematic diagnostic workup should precede any antimicrobial decision.

clinicalPearls: Current (post-Petersdorf) FUO definition requires all of: fever >=38.3C (101F) on at least two occasions, illness lasting at least 3 weeks, no known immunocompromised state, and a diagnosis still uncertain after thorough history, examination, and a defined set of obligatory investigations (p.149).
Inflammation of unknown origin (IUO) shares the FUO definition but lacks the temperature criterion (elevated CRP/ESR with normal temperature); its causes and workup are identical to FUO (p.149).
FUO usually reflects an ATYPICAL presentation of a COMMON disease rather than a rare disease; pattern recognition explains the higher diagnostic yield at expert centers (pp.150, 153).

The cornerstone of the workup is the search for potentially diagnostic clues (PDCs) - all localizing signs, symptoms, and abnormalities pointing toward a diagnosis - via repeated history, examination, and obligatory tests; further testing should be PDC-driven (pp.152-153).
Examination should pay special attention to the eyes, lymph nodes, temporal arteries, liver, spleen, prior surgical sites, the entire skin surface, and mucous membranes (p.152).

History should capture fever pattern (continuous vs recurrent) and duration, prior medical history, current/recent drugs, family and sexual history, country of origin, recent and remote travel, environmental/hobby exposures, and animal contacts (p.152).
Giant cell arteritis is notably prevalent among FUO patients, with rates up to 17% in the elderly; temporal artery biopsy is still recommended for patients >=55 years (p.153).
FUO with headache should prompt CSF microbiologic examination for herpes simplex virus (especially type 2), Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii, and M. tuberculosis (p.153).

In patients with recurrent/episodic FUO, ask the patient to return DURING a febrile episode; further tests should be done during an inflammatory episode since abnormalities may be absent between episodes (pp.152-153).

Geography shapes the differential: infections (especially TB) dominate non-Western cohorts, while noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs) are the most common cause in Western cohorts, accounting for up to one-third of cases (p.150).
Investigation of cryoglobulins is a useful low-cost screening test in FUO given the frequent absence of specific symptoms (p.153).
harrison.pathophysiology: FUO is a syndrome, not a single disease - a final prolonged febrile illness in which intensive standard evaluation has failed to localize a cause. Etiologies cluster into four groups: infections, noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs: autoimmune, autoinflammatory, granulomatous, and vasculitides), malignancy, and miscellaneous, with a substantial undiagnosed fraction. The spectrum has shifted over time: intraabdominal abscesses, tumors, and infective endocarditis have declined as CT, ultrasound, blood culture, and echocardiography improved, while entities such as acute HIV and autoinflammatory syndromes are now recognized. NIIDs may precede their typical clinical or laboratory features by months, requiring prolonged observation. The 'FUO paradox' describes how, despite better imaging (CT/MRI/PET-CT), the undiagnosed proportion is now higher (>50% in some Western cohorts) because most febrile illnesses are diagnosed before 3 weeks elapse, leaving only the most difficult cases to meet FUO criteria (pp.149-150).
additionalDifferentials: Infective endocarditis (including culture-negative endocarditis from fastidious organisms - nutritionally variant streptococci, HACEK group, Coxiella burnetii, Tropheryma whipplei, Bartonella) - one of the more common infectious causes (pp.150-151)
Extrapulmonary and miliary tuberculosis - up to half of infections in non-Western FUO are M. tuberculosis; miliary TB is especially hard to diagnose (pp.150, 153)
Q fever (Coxiella burnetii) - consider with rural exposure, animal contact, valve disease, aortic aneurysm, or vascular prosthesis; test by immunofluorescence assay (pp.150-151)
Whipple disease (Tropheryma whipplei) - consider with unexplained CNS, GI, or joint symptoms; PCR on stool and blood early (p.150)
Endemic infections after relevant travel/residence: malaria, visceral leishmaniasis, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis (p.150)
Adult-onset Still's disease (NIID, relatively common in FUO) (p.150)
Large-vessel vasculitis and giant cell arteritis / polymyalgia rheumatica (pp.150, 153)
Familial Mediterranean fever and other autoinflammatory syndromes (rare except in specific regions) (p.150)
Schnitzler's syndrome - urticaria, bone pain, monoclonal gammopathy (p.150)

VEXAS syndrome - adult-onset, middle-aged/elderly males, recurrent inflammation, chondritis, skin lesions, lung disease, venous thrombosis, arthritis, MDS; bone-marrow vacuoles in myeloid precursors; somatic UBA1 variants (p.150)
Malignant lymphoma - by far the most common neoplastic cause; fever may precede detectable lymphadenopathy (p.150)
Common solid tumors causing fever: breast, colon, hepatocellular, lung, pancreatic, renal cell carcinoma (p.151)
infectionMimics: Culture-negative endocarditis - sterile cultures may simply reflect ongoing antibiotic therapy rather than a noninfectious cause (pp.151-152)
Marantic (nonbacterial thrombotic) endocarditis - sterile, paraneoplastic, especially with adenocarcinomas, mimics infective endocarditis (p.151)
Sterile endocarditis of SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome (p.151)
nonInfectiousMimics: Drug-induced fever - virtually any drug, even after long-term use; common culprits include allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, sulfasalazine, furosemide, and antimicrobials (sulfonamides, minocycline, vancomycin, beta-lactams, isoniazid); fever persisting >72h after stopping the drug makes it an unlikely cause (pp.150, 153)
DRESS / drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome - often with eosinophilia and extensive lymphadenopathy (p.150)

Benign or exercise-induced hyperthermia - elevated temperature WITHOUT raised CRP/ESR or other inflammation; may be postinfectious (triggers similar to chronic fatigue syndrome: EBV, Q fever, COVID-19) (p.150)
Factitious fever - artificially induced (e.g., IV injection of contaminated water); suspect with access to medical equipment (p.150)
Fraudulent fever - patient is normothermic but manipulates the thermometer; simultaneous multi-site measurement (rectum/ear/mouth) and pulse-temperature dissociation are clues (p.150)
Central thermoregulatory disorders - brain tumor, stroke, encephalitis, hypothalamic dysfunction (p.151)
Peripheral thermoregulatory causes - hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, heat stroke (p.151)
additionalInvestigations: Obligatory baseline panel: ESR and CRP, platelet count, leukocyte count with differential, hemoglobin, electrolytes, creatinine, total protein, alkaline phosphatase, ALT, AST, LDH, creatine kinase, ferritin, antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, protein electrophoresis, urinalysis, three blood cultures, urine culture, chest x-ray, abdominal ultrasonography, and TST or IGRA (p.149)
Fundoscopy by an ophthalmologist - early, to exclude retinal vasculitis when PDCs are absent or misleading (p.153)

18F-FDG-PET/CT - established next step when PDC-guided tests are unrevealing; ~50% total diagnostic yield; best performed during active inflammation (elevated CRP/ESR or fever) and before glucocorticoids; outperforms gallium and labeled-leukocyte scintigraphy (pp.152-154)
Gallium-67 citrate or 111In/99mTc-labeled leukocyte scintigraphy - alternatives when PET/CT unavailable (lower yield; gallium localizes ~1/3, leukocyte ~1/5 of cases) (p.154)
Whole-body MRI - one study reported yield comparable to PET/CT (needs confirmation) (p.154)
Echocardiography - low yield without PDCs; reserve for high suspicion of endocarditis (p.153)
Liver biopsy (acid-fast smear, culture, PCR) - highest yield if miliary TB suspected; bone marrow / lymph node biopsies are alternatives (p.153)
Mycobacterial PCR alongside cultures - may shorten time to TB diagnosis (p.153)

Specialized blood cultures held long enough for fastidious organisms (e.g., HACEK); inform the lab and use special media for Histoplasma or Legionella; >3 blood cultures or >1 urine culture is useless without PDCs (p.153)
Q fever serology by immunofluorescence assay; T. whipplei PCR on stool/blood (pp.150-151)
Temporal artery biopsy in patients >=55 years for suspected giant cell arteritis (p.153)
CSF examination (HSV especially type 2, Cryptococcus, M. tuberculosis) when FUO is accompanied by headache (p.153)
Later-stage PDC-driven biopsies for pathology and/or microbiology (p.154)
redFlags: Clinical deterioration without new PDCs - the trigger to escalate workup (rather than wait) and the situation where empirical therapy may be justified (pp.152-153)
Hemodynamic instability or neutropenia - good indications for empirical antibiotic therapy (p.155)
Granulomatous disease on liver or bone marrow biopsy - should prompt (re)consideration of miliary tuberculosis (p.153)
Early phase of evaluation carries the highest FUO-related mortality risk (deaths occurred during index admission in cohort data; intravascular lymphoma and pneumonia found at autopsy) (p.154)
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis depends chiefly on the underlying diagnosis. When FUO remains unexplained after extensive evaluation, outlook is favorable: large cohorts report high rates of spontaneous fever resolution and mortality of 8% or less over several years of follow-up. The greatest mortality risk is during the early diagnostic phase. A normal 18F-FDG-PET/CT is associated with higher rates of spontaneous resolution and may help predict who will resolve. A symptom duration >12 months and a normal PET/CT both lower the chance of ever reaching a final diagnosis (pp.150, 154).
pitfalls: Starting empirical therapeutic trials before a diagnosis - should be AVOIDED except when the patient is rapidly deteriorating, because most undiagnosed patients resolve spontaneously (p.154).

Continuing antibiotics/glucocorticoids during workup - they mask disease: cultures become unreliable and glucocorticoids shrink lymph nodes regardless of cause; stop them before further testing (p.152).

Early empirical glucocorticoids - can mask fever while infection or lymphoma spreads and reduce the chance of diagnosing a treatable malignancy; avoid until infection and lymphoma are sufficiently excluded (p.155).

Ordering more screening tests without PDCs - low yield; immunologic and microbiologic serologies without PDCs more often give false-positives; better to wait for new PDCs unless the patient deteriorates (pp.153-154).
Over-culturing - performing >3 blood cultures or >1 urine culture is useless absent PDCs (p.153).
Failing to recognize PDCs already present in available information is a frequent cause of diagnostic delay (p.154).
Interpreting a negative TST/IGRA as excluding TB - it does not; results may be indeterminate in miliary TB, malnutrition, immunosuppression, or with anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies (p.153).

Misreading PET/CT - physiologic FDG uptake in brain, heart, bowel, kidneys, and bladder can obscure pathology (e.g., cardiac uptake masking endocarditis - mitigate with a pre-scan low-carbohydrate diet) (p.153).
Not excluding factitious/fraudulent fever and drug fever early, especially when inflammatory markers are normal (pp.150, 153).
harrison.severityClassification: FUO categories (by host/setting), each requiring a distinct approach: (1) classic FUO - the immunocompetent adult per the formal definition; (2) nosocomial FUO; (3) neutropenic FUO; and (4) HIV-associated FUO. The contemporary Harrison definition explicitly EXCLUDES immunocompromised states, which need a different, more aggressive approach. Etiologies are grouped into four diagnostic categories - infections, noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs), malignancy, and miscellaneous - with a large 'no diagnosis' fraction (pp.149-150).
